analysis:
The change is confined to .github/workflows/ci.yml. The single `test-provider` lane (count 5) is split into five per-shard lanes, `test-provider-1` through `test-provider-5`, each requesting 1 runner. The matrix job now selects its runner with `fromJSON(needs.route.outputs.routes)[format('test-provider-{0}', matrix.shard)]` (head line 142). This only changes how CI runners are chosen. It touches no provider runtime code, no coordinator-to-provider WebSocket contract (TB-002), no attestation or App Attest authorization (TB-009/TB-011), no cache-storage code (T-041), and no keys.

Workflow permissions are unchanged: top-level `contents: read`, and `route` still has `permissions: {}`. No new secrets, triggers, third-party actions or `pull_request_target` usage are introduced. The routing lanes still use read-only jobs, and the matrix shard value is a fixed integer list [1..5], so there is no attacker-controlled input in the lane-name expression.

One open integration question: the reusable workflow `darkbloom-route.yml` and `scripts/test-darkbloom-route.py` were not supplied, so I could not confirm how they handle the new lane names or a missing lane key. If the key is absent, the matrix job would fail or get an empty `runs-on`, which would be an availability or CI-gating issue rather than a security regression. The `provider-test-gate` job still requires the overall `test-provider` result to be success, so a failure there blocks the gate rather than bypassing it. Runner trust (Darkbloom Sandbox versus Blacksmith fallback) is as before: the lanes are read-only, but the per-shard grants may change which jobs land on sandbox Macs. That is a CI-infrastructure question, not a defined threat in this model.

No findings.
